short: An English architect, astronomer, and mathematician who rebuilt much of London, including St Paul's Cathedral, after the Great Fire.
full:
Sir Christopher Wren was one of the most highly acclaimed English architects in history, as well as a notable astronomer, mathematician, and physicist. A founding member of the Royal Society, his early career was dominated by scientific inquiry, earning him the admiration of figures such as Isaac Newton and Blaise Pascal. However, he found his most enduring calling in architecture, a discipline he largely taught himself through the study of Italian and French classical designs.

Wren's defining opportunity arose from the devastation of the Great Fire of London in 1666. He was tasked with rebuilding fifty-two of the city's ruined churches, culminating in his masterpiece, St Paul's Cathedral. Completed in 1711, its iconic dome transformed the London skyline and became a symbol of national resilience. Wren also designed numerous other monumental structures, including the Royal Hospital Chelsea, the Old Royal Naval College at Greenwich, and the south front of Hampton Court Palace, permanently stamping his English Baroque style on the nation's built environment.
